comparacoes.titulo: Obtaining the mapper: Mappers.getMapper/INSTANCE vs dependency injection

Mappers.getMapper + INSTANCE: Suitable when no DI framework is used; by convention the interface declares an INSTANCE field
Generated mappers are stateless and thread-safe, so they can be accessed by several threads
Injection via componentModel (cdi, sprin: The guide recommends obtaining mappers by injection when using CDI or Spring, instead of the Mappers class
Mappers used via `uses` are obtained through the same component model (they must be beans)

comparacoes.titulo: MapStruct injection strategies: field vs constructor vs setter

FIELD (default): It is the current default; it can be changed through a processor option
CONSTRUCTOR: The guide recommends constructor injection to simplify tests
With CDI a default constructor is also generated
SETTER: Use it when there are circular dependencies in Spring (compilation may fail with a constructor)
For abstract classes or decorators, setter injection must be used

texto_nao_diz: Spring Boot rules beyond those cited

comparacoes.titulo: Mapper as an interface (default methods) vs abstract class

Interface with default methods: Available with Java 8+; the generated code invokes the manual method if the types match
Abstract class: Allows declaring additional fields in the mapper
For abstract classes or decorators, use setter injection

comparacoes.titulo: Where to put manual logic in MapStruct: default method, uses, expression, @AfterMapping, decorator

default method / abstract method in a cl: Manual logic directly in the mapper for one pair of types
uses (another class): Manual mapper/method in another class; in the default model it needs a public no-argument constructor
expression / defaultExpression: Inline Java expressions; they are not validated at generation time and require imports
@BeforeMapping/@AfterMapping: Callbacks for all applicable methods; the order within the same type is not guaranteed
@DecoratedWith: Typed customization of specific methods; with CDI the guide says to use CDI decorators

texto_nao_diz: objective criterion for choosing among the options (the guide only describes each one)

comparacoes.titulo: How MapStruct instantiates the target: builder vs constructor vs setters/fields

Builder: Used automatically if the BuilderProvider finds one; it can be turned off (disableBuilder / mapstruct.disableBuilders)
Constructor: Without a builder, it looks for @Default > single public constructor > no-argument constructor; ambiguity is an error
Setters/public fields: Public fields serve as accessors when there is no getter/setter

ACCESSOR_ONLY: Uses setters or getters (equivalent to DEFAULT); on update it clears and repopulates
SETTER_PREFERRED: Prefers setters; uses adders if there is only an adder and getters if there is none (table)
ADDER_PREFERRED: Prefers adders; typical of generated JPA entities; on update it does not clear
TARGET_IMMUTABLE: Uses setters; according to the table, throws an exception when the target has only an adder or no accessor

texto_nao_diz: which @Mapper attribute defines the strategy (the guide only names the type)

Reactive: Non-blocking model with streams; scenarios: real-time UIs, complex networks, microservices, IoT/streaming
Requires testing with WebTestClient and configuring reactive security
Traditional: Operations are processed one at a time (blocking); scales by adding servers

texto_nao_diz: the book states that the decision is not to use the newest option but to fit the needs (p.77)

comparacoes.titulo: HTTP clients: RestTemplate vs WebClient vs Feign

RestTemplate: Traditional, synchronous; requires more code per call (according to the book)
WebClient: Part of WebFlux, asynchronous; steeper learning curve without familiarity with reactive
Feign: Declarative client via an interface, `@FeignClient`; RestTemplate-like simplicity with a modern approach

comparacoes.titulo: Building an image: layered jar vs Cloud Native Buildpacks

Layered jar: Separates dependencies and application into layers to reuse the Docker cache (layers.idx)
The book does not show the plugin configuration to enable it
Buildpacks (bootBuildImage): Builds the image without writing a Dockerfile; command ./gradlew bootBuildImage --imageName=demoapp

MongoDB: Unstructured/semi-structured data with flexibility; reviews (Review) as documents
Hybrid model: The project uses both: Postgres for books/authors/publishers and Mongo for reviews

@CacheEvict(allEntries = true): Used in POST and PUT to clear all entries of the "books" cache
@CacheEvict(key = \"#id\"): Used on removal to clear only the book's entry

ddl-auto=update: Used in the example to generate/update the schema from the entities
Liquibase: Versioned changelog (YAML/XML/JSON/SQL), applied at startup; includeAll in alphabetical order

ConfigMap: Separates configuration from the image; injected as an environment variable
Profiles (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE): application-prod/test.properties and an environment variable activate the profile

comparacoes.titulo: Test types in the book: unit (Mockito) vs @WebMvcTest vs integration (Testcontainers/WireMock) vs reactive

@WebMvcTest + @WithMockUser: Only the web layer and the imported security configuration; service and JwtDecoder mocked
Integration: Testcontainers (Postgres, Mongo) + WireMock (OIDC); without mocking the service/repository

comparacoes.titulo: Authentication in the example: HTTP Basic vs OAuth2 resource server with JWT

HTTP Basic: Simple, stateless initial configuration (username/password on every request)
OAuth2 resource server (JWT) with Keyclo: Validates JWTs issued by Keycloak; RBAC by roles from the realm_access claim
The access token expires in 300 s in the example

comparacoes.titulo: CQRS vs Event Sourcing vs Saga (SB3G ch.2)

CQRS: Separates writes (commands) from reads (queries); only worthwhile if the load is unbalanced
Event Sourcing: Stores each change as an immutable event and rebuilds state by replay; good for auditing
Saga: Splits a distributed transaction into local transactions with compensation
